ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Peoria, IL
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Peoria, Illinois machinery plants, grain facilities, boilers and tanks, on site. Request a UT quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Peoria, Illinois
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection for Peoria, Illinois owners: heavy-equipment fabrication and machining plants, grain and agricultural processing facilities, boilers and pressure vessels, aboveground tanks, river-front structures and structural steel. Crews travel to your Peoria facility carrying calibrated gauges and flaw detectors, follow a written procedure, and write up results against whichever code your contract cites. Request a UT inspection quote for your Peoria site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic inspection is used in Peoria

Peoria sits on bluffs above the Illinois River in the middle of corn and soybean country, and the city's economy reflects both. Heavy machinery and agricultural equipment manufacturing has long been the backbone of the area, alongside metal products and chemicals, while the river, four Class I railroads and the interstate bridges make it a freight and grain-handling hub. Large hospital systems add central-plant steam and hot-water piping to the mix. Each of these produces steel that wears, corrodes or cracks in its own way, and each calls for ultrasonic work.

Examples of UT scopes in this market:

  • Weld examination on thick-section fabrications, frames and booms built by machinery manufacturers.
  • Wall surveys on steam, condensate and compressed-air systems in large manufacturing plants.
  • Thickness readings on dryers, bins, hoppers, process vessels and piping in grain and agricultural processing.
  • Shell and floor thickness on aboveground storage tanks at terminals and plants.
  • Pressure vessels, deaerators and boilers in hospital and industrial central plants.
  • Structural steel groove welds and bridge-related repairs in a city that depends on its river crossings.

What UT finds and what it misses

Ultrasonic testing uses a short pulse of high-frequency sound. In thickness work the instrument times the echo from the back wall and converts it to remaining metal. In weld work an angled probe sends shear waves through the joint and a flaw reflects part of the sound back, showing up as a signal between the entry point and the back wall. That ability to look inside metal makes UT the method for corrosion loss, laminations, lack of fusion, slag and internal cracks.

Several conditions limit it. Scale, heavy paint and rough weld caps scatter sound and prevent a clean reading. Deep pitting can fool a single-element gauge into reporting more metal than is there. Coarse cast structures and austenitic welds attenuate the beam. A gauge reads one spot at a time, so a survey is only as complete as its grid, and tight crack-like flaws that lie parallel to the sound path can be missed without a second scan angle. The report states these conditions where they apply.

Codes, standards and the Illinois regime

Thickness work follows ASTM E797 and the thickness provisions of ASME Section V, summarized in the Article 5 and thickness requirements guide. Weld examination is written to Section V Article 4 and judged against the code that built the item: ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessel welds, ASME B31.1 for power piping, or AWS D1.1 Clause 8 for structural steel. Existing tanks and vessels are often managed under API 653 and API 510, in which the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection and our role is to supply the thickness and flaw data.

In Illinois, boilers and pressure vessels are regulated under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, administered by the Division of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety in the Office of the State Fire Marshal. The Act has the chief inspector, deputy inspectors or commissioned special inspectors inspect covered equipment, adopts the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, the National Board Inspection Code and API standards, and requires an inspection certificate to be posted at the equipment. Exemptions exist, for example for vessels used solely in agriculture, so owners should confirm which of their equipment is covered.

How the work is done

Thickness jobs begin by calibrating the gauge on a step block of the same alloy as the item. Where the inner surface is corroded, we use a dual-element probe because it copes with pitting better than a single crystal. Readings are taken on a marked grid or at the owner's condition monitoring locations, with the A-scan watched wherever a value looks odd. Hot surfaces call for high-temperature probes and couplant plus a temperature correction.

Weld jobs use a reference built from side-drilled holes, angle-beam scanning at 45, 60 or 70 degrees from both sides of the weld where possible, and sizing of any reflector above the recording level. Indications are plotted by position along the weld, depth and length, and compared with the acceptance table in the governing code.

Surface condition on river-city steel

Steel that lives near a river, in grain dust or in outdoor storage collects scale, dust and layered paint. Grain dust forms a hard crust when damp, and outdoor equipment in a humid climate develops flaking coatings that hold air. The result is poor coupling, so test points are cleaned with a wire brush, scraper or light grinding before readings begin. Coated surfaces can sometimes be read directly when the coating is sound and the procedure covers it, but loose coating is always removed locally.

Insulated vessels and lines need the owner to open insulation at each test point. Where the insulation hides corrosion, the readings often show the worst loss close to the opening, which is why test points are often chosen at low spots and at supports.

Coated and insulated equipment

Much Peoria equipment wears paint, lining or insulation. Where a sound coating is fully bonded and the procedure has been demonstrated through it, readings may be taken without stripping it, and the report notes that the coating was present. Insulated lines are different: the owner opens a window at each test point, and the technician measures in the hidden area where wet insulation tends to cause worst-case corrosion, then asks the owner to restore the jacket and sealant.

Calibration and verification during a survey

A gauge is only as good as its last check. At the start of a Peoria survey the technician calibrates on a step block of matching material, confirms the reading on a second step, and logs the gauge, probe and block serial numbers. The same check is repeated whenever the probe or cable is changed and again at the end. If the closing check has drifted, readings since the last good check are repeated instead of corrected on paper, which keeps the data defensible when an inspector or insurer reviews it.

Trending readings between outages

One survey shows where the wall is today; two surveys show how fast it is going. Each test point is marked with a durable identifier and recorded on the grid sheet, and later visits use the same points and the same technique so numbers compare cleanly. Where an owner already keeps condition monitoring locations in a database, we adopt their numbering and return data in their layout. Any point that reads thicker than last time is flagged for review instead of quietly accepted, since a rising value usually means a different probe position or a surface problem rather than metal growth.

Who performs and reviews the work

The Peoria work is staffed by crews who travel in for each agreed scope. Qualification is issued through the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician calibrates, scans and interprets, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. If your company has its own written practice, we can follow it. Our Level III consulting and written practice development pages describe the help available when procedures need to be written or aligned.

What the UT report contains

A report names the item or line number, the drawing or isometric reference, material and nominal wall, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe, couplant and calibration block, the technician and level, and the date. Thickness reports provide a map or grid with each reading, the minimum value found, and a flag for any point under the owner's alert or retirement thickness. Weld reports provide a scan sketch with the location, amplitude, length and depth of each reflector and an accept or reject decision against the named criteria. Readings can be returned as a spreadsheet for trending.

Typical UT scopes and the references behind them

Common ultrasonic scopes for Peoria-area owners
ComponentWhat the technician recordsTypical reference
Machinery frames and boomsInternal weld flaws in thick sectionsAWS D1.1, ASME Section V Article 4
Steam and condensate pipingWall at elbows and low pointsASTM E797, ASME B31.1
Grain and process vesselsShell thickness and corrosion lossASME Section VIII, API 510
Aboveground tanksShell courses and floor plateAPI 653
Hospital central plantsBoiler and vessel wallNBIC, ASME Section V
Bridge and structural steelGroove weld flawsAWS D1.5, AWS D1.1

Planning a UT job in Peoria

Peoria winters are properly cold: the average January low is about 17 degrees Fahrenheit, snowfall averages around two feet a year, and relative humidity runs highest in winter. Summers are warm, with July highs near 86. Cold stiffens couplant and drains battery life in gauges, so we pick couplant for the surface temperature and keep calibration blocks at the same temperature as the work. Frost and ice on outdoor tanks and structural steel must be cleared before any reading, and wind exposure on tall steel affects how long a technician can work in one place.

Grain-handling and processing sites have seasonal peaks around harvest, and their maintenance windows tend to fall outside them, so UT scopes are usually planned for off-season shutdowns. Dust-classified areas call for site permits and instruments allowed in the area; the quote asks about hazard classification up front. Plant orientation, badges and lockout rules apply everywhere, and river-front sites may add flood-season access constraints.

UT, MT or PT for your Peoria job

Choose UT for remaining wall and internal weld flaws. When the concern is a surface crack in carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Peoria is quicker, and for stainless steel, aluminum or other non-magnetic parts, liquid penetrant testing in Peoria applies. Shutdown scopes often use all three on a single vessel. The national ultrasonic testing page and the ultrasonic testing guide go deeper, and the Illinois inspection services page shows how Atlantis services combine across the state.

Training your own UT technicians

Owners who prefer in-house capability can use the UT Level 1 course and UT Level 2 course, practice on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator and review the SNT-TC-1A eligibility guide. Area details sit on the Peoria NDT training page. The employer issues the qualification, not the course provider.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness testing on grain processing equipment in Peoria?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to the site, clean the test points, and measure dryers, bins, vessels and piping on a marked grid, returning a thickness map with the minimum reading flagged against your alert level.

faq.q: Do you inspect boilers and pressure vessels covered by the Illinois Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act?
faq.a: We collect thickness and weld-flaw data on that equipment. The commissioned inspector remains responsible for the statutory inspection and certificate, and our data supports the inspector's decision.

faq.q: Can UT examine thick welds on heavy equipment frames?
faq.a: Yes. Angle-beam shear-wave scanning examines the weld volume in thick sections, using a reference built from side-drilled holes, and reports lack of fusion, slag and cracks against AWS D1.1 or the contract criteria.

faq.q: How do you handle cold weather UT in a Peoria winter?
faq.a: Couplant is chosen for the surface temperature, calibration blocks are kept at the same temperature as the work, ice and frost are cleared, and extreme cold may mean rescheduling for a milder window.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a weld?
faq.a: Only where the construction code, the owner and the engineer agree beforehand. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain their own UT provisions, and each substitution is settled before the job starts.

faq.q: What happens if a surface is too rough or coated for a reading?
faq.a: Loose scale and flaking paint are removed at the test point. Sound coatings may be read through if the procedure covers it; otherwise the point is cleaned, and any location we cannot read is listed in the report.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Peoria?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Peoria. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and the quote comes from your drawings, access notes and the governing code.

faq.q: Can our maintenance team learn UT from Atlantis courses?
faq.a: Yes. The UT Level 1 and Level 2 courses and the practical simulator prepare candidates, and your company then qualifies them under its written practice based on SNT-TC-1A.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection & MT Testing | Peoria, IL
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection for Peoria, Illinois machinery welds, castings, crane gear and bridge steel, on your site. Request an MPI quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Peoria, Illinois
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection on carbon and low-alloy steel for Peoria, Illinois owners: welded frames and booms from heavy-equipment manufacturing, castings and forgings, crane and rigging components, grain-facility steelwork, bridge and structural connections, and repair welds on boilers and vessels. Crews travel to your Peoria facility carrying yokes, particles, a light meter and field indicators, follow a written procedure, and write up results against whichever code your contract cites. Request a mag particle testing quote for your Peoria site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used around Peoria

Peoria is a machine-building city. Companies that make earthmoving and agricultural equipment have shaped its steel economy for generations, and the supply chain around them includes foundries, forge shops, weld fabricators and machine shops. The same region moves grain by river and rail, runs large hospital central plants, and relies on a handful of river bridges. Heavy equipment is dynamically loaded and welded from thick plate, so fatigue cracks at weld toes and stress concentrations are the everyday damage mechanism, and those cracks begin on the surface, where magnetic particle inspection is strongest.

Examples of MT work in this market:

  • Weld toes and root-side repairs on frames, booms, buckets and chassis structures during fabrication and rebuild.
  • Castings and forgings, including gear blanks, axle housings and large machined parts, before and after machining.
  • Hooks, lugs, chains and below-the-hook devices on cranes and hoists in plants and yards.
  • Structural steel in elevators, conveyors, legs and galleries at grain handling and processing facilities.
  • Bridge and structural steel connections where AWS weld examination is called for.
  • Excavations and finished repair welds on boilers, receivers and process vessels.

What magnetic particle inspection finds, and what it misses

Magnetizing a steel part makes any crack or seam that reaches the surface leak flux, and fine ferrous particles gather at the leak, drawing the flaw as a line you can see. The method works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon and low-alloy steels and martensitic grades qualify, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper do not. It is sensitive to surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities and loses sensitivity quickly with depth.

It cannot measure wall thickness, find deep internal flaws, or reveal a crack that lies along the field direction, which is why two orientations are required. Surface preparation is also part of the method: heavy scale, oil and thick paint block particle build-up and are removed first. On large castings and thick welds, the technician may need to move the yoke across overlapping positions to cover the whole surface, which takes time that a quote should allow for.

Codes and acceptance criteria that govern MT work

MT is written to ASME Section V Article 7, set out in our Article 7 explainer, together with ASTM E1444 and ASTM E709. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for bridge welds. Work on equipment managed under API 510, 570 or 653 follows the construction code, with the owner's authorized inspector remaining responsible for the inspection.

Illinois covers boilers and pressure vessels through the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, administered by the Division of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety within the Office of the State Fire Marshal. The Act adopts the ASME Code and the National Board Inspection Code and sets rules for repair and alteration, so MT of a repair weld on registered equipment often forms part of the file the commissioned inspector reviews.

How the examination is done

Field work usually uses an electromagnetic yoke. The AC yoke meets the lifting-power check in Article 7 for surface examination, and DC or permanent-magnet yokes need a higher pull to qualify. Prods, coils and cables are options where a yoke cannot reach, as the procedure allows. Dry powder is the choice on hot, rough or field-welded surfaces; wet visible and wet fluorescent suspensions deliver more sensitivity on cleaned machined parts, and fluorescent work requires a darkened area with a measured UV-A source.

The technician verifies field strength with a pie gauge or shim, applies particles during magnetization, inspects overlapping zones, then repeats at a second orientation. Where a leftover field would harm later machining, welding or bearing life, the part is demagnetized and checked with a gauss meter.

Foundry, forge and fabrication shop work

Parts brought to a bench or booth are easier to examine than assemblies left in place, because they can be cleaned, magnetized in several directions with a stationary unit and lit properly. Casting examination looks for hot tears, shrinkage cracks and cold laps; forgings for laps and seams; machined parts for grinding cracks and heat-treatment cracks. We take care to separate real cracks from non-relevant indications at sharp corners, keyways and thread roots, where flux naturally concentrates, so owners do not scrap good parts.

For weld fabrication, the examination is staged: after root or hot pass where the code requires, after back-gouging, and after the final pass and any post-weld heat treatment, since heat treatment itself can crack heavy sections. Each stage is a separate record.

Lifting equipment and fatigue-prone steel

Hooks, chains, lugs and spreader beams carry the load that hurts people when they fail, and they are a frequent reason Peoria owners call for mag particle work. Hooks crack at the saddle and shank, lugs crack at the pin-hole edge, and welded attachments crack at their toes. The examination normally supports a periodic inspection program set by the owner's engineer or crane inspector. We examine the load-bearing zones the program names, record each item by tag, and report rejectable indications so that the item stays out of service until it is repaired or replaced.

Fatigue also appears in conveyor supports, vibrating equipment skids and bridge-related connections, where repeated cycles open cracks slowly. These are worth re-examining at intervals chosen from the first findings.

Preparing surfaces and judging indications

Bare, dry steel gives clearer results, so spatter, loose scale, grease and thick paint are removed from the examination area and a short distance beyond each weld. Contrast paint helps dry and wet visible particles show against dark steel. Not every particle line is a flaw: magnetic writing, changes of section and weld edges produce non-relevant lines, while dirt and lint cause false ones. The technician separates them by re-cleaning, remagnetizing and, where needed, trying another field direction.

Only relevant indications are measured against the acceptance limits. Linear, rounded and clustered indications are judged differently by most codes, so the report states shape and size, which lets the owner's engineer choose whether to grind, repair or accept.

Who performs and reviews the work

Peoria jobs are staffed by examiners who travel in for each agreed scope. Their qualifications come through the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. If your company holds its own written practice, we can follow it, and the written practice development and Level III consulting pages describe how procedures are built or aligned.

Staged examination during weld fabrication

On heavy fabrications the examination is often staged: after the root or hot pass where the code requires it, after back-gouging, after the final pass, and again after any post-weld heat treatment, since stress relief can itself open cracks in thick sections. Each stage is its own record, so a rejected indication can be traced to the weld step that produced it.

Documenting and demagnetizing

Parts that have been magnetized can hold a residual field that attracts chips, disturbs arc welding or accelerates bearing wear. When the procedure or the owner requires it, the part is demagnetized and measured with a gauss meter, and the reading is recorded. Large welded assemblies often need no demagnetizing unless they will be welded or machined next, and the quote says which applies.

What the MT report contains

The report names the part or weld identifier, drawing, material and surface condition, the procedure and revision, equipment and calibration status, the technique used, field verification, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is located, oriented and sized, and judged against the named acceptance criteria. Sketches or photos accompany rejectable indications, and the record states whether demagnetization was done and verified.

Typical MT scopes and the references behind them

Common magnetic particle scopes for Peoria-area owners
ComponentWhat is examinedTypical reference
Heavy-equipment frames and boomsWeld toes and stress-concentration cracksAWS D1.1, ASTM E1444
Castings and forgingsHot tears, laps and seamsASTM E709, owner specification
Crane hooks and lifting gearSaddle, shank and pin-hole cracksASME Section V Article 7
Grain facility structural steelConnection and support weldsAWS D1.1
Bridge steel connectionsFillet and groove weldsAWS D1.5
Boiler and vessel repairsExcavations and repair weldsASME Section VIII Appendix 6, NBIC

Planning a magnetic particle job in Peoria

Peoria's average January low is close to 17 degrees Fahrenheit and snow is frequent, so outdoor mag particle work on frames, towers and bridge steel has to deal with frost, snow and cold steel. Wet suspensions can freeze or lose contrast, particle carriers behave differently, and dry powder is often chosen for cold field work. In summer, with July highs near 86 and high humidity, dew and sweating on steel can affect particle adhesion until surfaces are dried. Wind blows dry powder away, so shelter or a different technique may be needed on exposed structures.

Plant schedules matter: heavy-equipment lines run in shifts, and grain facilities have harvest peaks, so MT is typically arranged for planned downtime. Expect safety orientation, lockout, hot-work and, in grain areas, hazard classification checks. Fluorescent examination needs shade; on an open floor that usually means a booth. The quote lists what the owner is asked to provide, such as clean access and lighting.

MT, PT or UT for your Peoria job

Use MT as the quick surface check on carbon and low-alloy steel. If a part is stainless, aluminum or another non-magnetic alloy, liquid penetrant testing in Peoria is the surface method, and for wall loss or internal weld flaws ultrasonic testing in Peoria is the right choice. The national magnetic particle testing page, the complete MT guide and the MT versus PT comparison help with the selection, and the Illinois inspection services page shows how the services combine.

Training your own MT technicians

Companies that want in-house mag particle capability can begin with the MT Level 1 course and continue to the MT Level 2 course, using the NDT practice tests for preparation. Local details are on the Peoria NDT training page. The employer issues the qualification under its written practice, which is how SNT-TC-1A is designed to work.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done on heavy equipment frames in Peoria?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your plant or yard and examine weld toes, repair excavations and stress-concentration areas on frames and booms with portable yokes, within the limits of surface condition and access.

faq.q: Do you inspect castings and forgings?
faq.a: Yes, where they can be cleaned and magnetized. Examination looks for hot tears, shrinkage cracks, laps and seams, and it separates relevant indications from non-relevant ones at corners, keyways and thread roots.

faq.q: Which materials can MT examine?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials such as carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper cannot be magnetized, so liquid penetrant testing is used for those.

faq.q: Can you do MT outdoors in a Peoria winter?
faq.a: Often, with changes. Dry powder or a cold-rated suspension is used, frost and snow are cleared, and extreme cold or wind may mean the work is moved to a better window.

faq.q: Why must a part be examined in two directions?
faq.a: A crack running parallel to the magnetic field leaks almost no flux and may not show. Magnetizing again at roughly ninety degrees ensures that cracks in either direction are detected.

faq.q: Do you check crane hooks and rigging?
faq.a: Yes. Hooks, lugs, chains and below-the-hook devices are examined at load-bearing zones and welds, using the criteria in the owner's procedure or the standard that applies to the equipment.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Peoria office?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Peoria. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and your quote is based on your drawings, access conditions and the code that applies.

faq.q: Can our staff learn MT through Atlantis courses?
faq.a: Yes. The MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses prepare candidates, and your company qualifies them under its written practice based on SNT-TC-1A. The final qualification comes from the employer.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant | Peoria, IL
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection in Peoria, Illinois for stainless steel, aluminum, welds and castings, on your site. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Peoria, Illinois
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, for Peoria, Illinois owners who need surface cracks found in materials a magnet cannot examine: stainless steel in food and chemical processing, aluminum parts, nickel alloys, welds, castings and machined components. Crews travel to your Peoria facility carrying penetrant, cleaners, developer and lighting, follow a written procedure, and write up results against whichever code your contract cites. Request a dye penetrant inspection quote for your Peoria site and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used around Peoria

Peoria's mix of machinery plants, agricultural processing, chemicals and hospitals uses plenty of non-ferrous and stainless material. Agricultural and food processors build with stainless steel for hygiene; chemical plants use stainless and nickel alloys against corrosion; machinery makers fabricate aluminum guards, housings and cooling components; and hospital central plants run stainless and copper piping. For all of these, PT is the straightforward way to confirm that welds and machined surfaces are free of cracks open to the surface.

Examples of PT work in this market:

  • Stainless welds on tanks, piping, heat exchangers and conveyors in agricultural and food processing plants.
  • Repair welds on stainless and duplex process vessels in chemical operations before return to service.
  • Aluminum and non-ferrous welded fabrications, from guards and housings to cooling-system parts.
  • Machined components and castings, such as valve bodies, pump parts and hydraulic fittings, checked for open cracks and laps.
  • Socket welds and small-bore connections where geometry blocks other methods.
  • Non-magnetic repair work on equipment rebuilds in machinery and component shops.

What penetrant testing finds, and what it misses

PT reveals discontinuities that break the surface. A low-viscosity dye, either a red visible type or a fluorescent type, is drawn into cracks, seams, laps and pores by capillary action. The excess is removed, a developer pulls the trapped dye back out, and the flaw appears as a clear, bright bleed-out. It works on any non-porous material and needs no power source, so it is practical in the field.

The method has hard limits. A defect must be open and clean for penetrant to enter, so cracks smeared shut by grinding, blasting or machining, or filled with oil, paint or scale, can pass unseen. Porous materials trap dye and mask indications. PT detects nothing below the surface and says nothing about wall thickness. Because the cleaning step often decides the result, a reputable procedure treats it as seriously as the penetrant itself.

Codes and acceptance criteria that govern PT work

PT is written to ASME Section V Article 6, as set out in the Article 6 explainer, with ASTM E165 as the general industry practice. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.6 for structural and stainless fabrication. Work on equipment under API 510, 570 or 653 follows the construction code, and the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection while we supply the examination results.

On austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, the penetrant, cleaner and developer must be low in chlorine, fluorine and sulfur, since residues can cause cracking in service. We check lot certificates against the procedure limit before the job begins, which owners with such alloys should always expect.

In Illinois, boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, enforced by the Division of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety in the Office of the State Fire Marshal, which adopts the ASME Code and the National Board Inspection Code. PT of repair welds on covered equipment often belongs to the record that the commissioned inspector reviews.

How the examination is done

The area is pre-cleaned and fully dried, since penetrant cannot enter a wet or dirty flaw. Penetrant is applied by brush, spray or immersion and left to dwell for the period in the procedure, which depends on material, type of flaw and temperature. Solvent-removable systems are wiped with dampened cloths; water-washable systems are rinsed under controlled spray. A thin, even coat of developer follows, and after the developing time the surface is examined under white light for visible dye, or under UV-A light in a dark enclosure for fluorescent dye, with intensity checked by meter.

Indications are measured and compared with the acceptance criteria, then the part is cleaned of residue. That final cleaning is important on stainless parts, on components that will be welded or coated, and on hydraulic or lubricated equipment, where leftover penetrant would contaminate the system.

Cold, damp and bright conditions in the Midwest

Penetrant materials are used within a standard window of about 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit at the surface. Below that, the liquid thickens and enters flaws slowly; above it, solvents flash off before the dwell is complete. Peoria's average January low sits near 17 degrees, so outdoor steel often sits well under the lower limit for months, and the procedure either has to be demonstrated at the lower temperature on a test panel or the work moved to a warm space. Sun-heated stainless in July, with highs near 86 and high humidity, can exceed the upper limit, so surface temperature is measured with a contact thermometer before the dye goes on.

Damp, humid air slows drying and can leave moisture in crack mouths, and strong sunlight can wash out visible dye. A shaded area or a tent solves most of it. Fluorescent PT requires darkness, so on an open plant floor a portable booth is normally used.

Removal systems and how they are chosen

Solvent-removable penetrant is wiped off with dampened cloths and suits welds and local areas in the field, because it needs no water supply or drain. Water-washable penetrant is rinsed with controlled spray and is quicker on large, rough parts, though easier to over-wash. Post-emulsifiable systems add an emulsifier step for high sensitivity on production parts but need a proper station. For most on-site Peoria work, a solvent-removable system with a non-aqueous developer is the practical choice, and the procedure names the system so the result can be repeated.

Telling real flaws from false ones

Dye on a surface does not always mean a crack. A round spot at a weld toe may be porosity, a thin line may be a crack or seam, and a general haze usually means excess penetrant was not fully removed. When the cause is unclear, the area is cleaned and re-tested, because a true flaw returns in the same place with the same shape. Relevant indications are measured and compared with the code's limits, where linear indications face tighter limits than rounded ones, so the report states orientation and length as well as position.

Who performs and reviews the work

Examiners are mobilized from outside the city for each Peoria scope. Qualification comes through the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician applies the method and interprets indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. If your company has its own procedures, we can work to them, and the Level III consulting and written practice development pages describe how procedures are developed or reconciled.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the component or weld, drawing, material and surface finish, the procedure and revision, the penetrant family and lot numbers, the cleaner and developer, and the pre-cleaning method. It records surface temperature, dwell and developing times, the lighting and its measured intensity, the technician and level, and the date. Each indication is located and sized and judged as accept or reject against the named code. Photographs of rejectable indications are included, and post-cleaning is noted.

Typical PT scopes and the references behind them

Surface preparation and etching

Grinding, wire brushing, blasting and machining can all smear metal over a crack mouth and seal it. A part that needs PT after such work may require an etch, a rinse and a full dry before penetrant goes on, and the procedure should say so. Oil, grease, scale and paint are removed first with the proper cleaner or mechanical means. On stainless equipment from food and agricultural processing, protein films, sugars and mineral deposits are removed as well, because they hold dye and give false indications.

Post-cleaning and handover

Penetrant residue left on a part can contaminate a hydraulic circuit, interfere with a later weld, or sit in a crevice on stainless steel. After examination the area is cleaned with a suitable solvent and wiped dry, developer is removed from machined surfaces and threads, and the technician confirms the cleaning in the record. Where the owner needs a clean-room or food-contact surface returned, the cleaning method is agreed in advance so no unapproved solvent touches the equipment.

Handover includes marked-up sketches showing where each indication sits, so a repair crew can find it without searching, plus photographs taken before the developer was removed.

Equipment that cannot be taken apart

Large Peoria vessels, conveyors and welded frames are examined where they stand, so staging, access and lighting come first. The technician sets up shade or a tent against sun and drafts, protects nearby product and coatings from overspray, and uses aerosol systems that keep solvent use low in occupied buildings. Where confined-space entry is required, the owner's permit system governs, and the quote lists what the owner provides.

PT, MT or UT for your Peoria job

Pick PT for non-magnetic materials and for cracks open to the surface where a yoke will not work. For carbon and low-alloy steel, magnetic particle inspection in Peoria is faster and finds slightly subsurface flaws as well, and for wall loss or internal weld defects ultrasonic testing in Peoria is the correct tool. The national penetrant testing page and the MT versus PT comparison explain the difference, and the Illinois inspection services page shows how the methods fit one scope.

Companies that want in-house penetrant capability can start with the PT Level 1 course and PT Level 2 course and rehearse on the Practical NDT penetrant simulator. Details for the area are on the Peoria NDT training page. The employer issues qualification under its written practice.

faq.q: What materials can liquid penetrant testing inspect in Peoria plants?
faq.a: Any clean, non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, brass and carbon steel. It reveals only discontinuities open to the surface, such as cracks, laps and pores.

faq.q: When should I choose PT over magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Choose PT for non-magnetic materials such as austenitic stainless steel and aluminum, or when the shape makes yoke magnetization impractical. On carbon steel, MT is often quicker and also catches slightly subsurface flaws.

faq.q: Can PT be done outdoors in a Peoria winter?
faq.a: Only if the surface is within the procedure's temperature range. Colder steel needs a procedure demonstrated at that temperature, or the work moves to a warmer space, because penetrant behaves differently when cold.

faq.q: Why does cleaning decide the result?
faq.a: Penetrant cannot enter flaws blocked by oil, paint, scale, moisture or smeared metal. Poor cleaning hides real cracks, so the procedure requires pre-cleaning and drying before any penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Do you control chlorine and sulfur for stainless work?
faq.a: Yes. Lot certificates are checked against the halogen and sulfur limits in the procedure before the materials are used on stainless or nickel alloys, and residues are removed after examination.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye is read under white light and suits field work. Fluorescent dye is read under UV-A light in a darkened area and shows finer indications, so it is used where more sensitivity is needed.
